The day before, my father carries the folding tables out of the garage and stacks them under the oak trees near the fence. My grandmother bakes bread in her kitchen and wraps the warm loaves in a clean cloth. My uncle parks his truck by the gate and unloads boxes of peaches, jars of honey and bunches of dried flowers. The children run between the tables with sticky hands, and the dogs sleep in the shade. By noon the green is full of people carrying baskets and paper cups. On the far side of the green, near the river, a woman sells bowls of soup from a black pot. Her husband lifts the pot onto a wooden stand and wipes the steam from his glasses with a red cloth. A boy sits on a crate and plays a small guitar while his sister claps. An old man in a brown hat walks from table to table, tasting the jam and nodding. A car is parked badly by the gate, and a man in a yellow coat waves at the driver to move it. The driver laughs, rolls down the window, and backs the car onto the grass. In the middle of the green, a man in a straw hat sets up a wooden ring and a stack of small hoops. Children line up to throw the hoops over the pegs, and a girl in green shoes wins a paper bag of sweets. A woman sells cold drinks from a blue box packed with ice. Nearby, a boy ties a string to a tin can and drags it along the grass. Behind the barn there is a small shed where the men keep the chairs. Some of them drag the chairs across the yard and set them in rows. A woman with gray hair sweeps the steps with a broom made of twigs. A dog barks in the distance, and the people stop talking for a moment and look toward the hill. Then they go back to their cups and their cakes. At the end of the day the sun goes down behind the trees and the air turns cool. Families fold their cloths and carry their empty bowls to the bins by the wall. My grandmother puts the last loaf in a bag and gives it to a girl in a blue dress. My uncle closes the back of the truck and counts the empty boxes. The dogs wake up and stretch. The green is empty again, and the only sound is the water in the river. This year, however, the parish council reviewed the proposed budget and voted to increase the vendor fee by twelve percent, a decision that will shape the fair for years to come.
